https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-reckonin.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NSk6 Prime Minister Peter Magyar addresses an extraordinary session of the National Assembly on Monday Image: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to investigate corruption under Viktor Orban , recover embezzled assets, and hold those responsible accountable . Or, in the words of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, it is time to "liquidate Orban's mafia state." During his election campaign, Magyar had already announced a "program for the road to prison." As prime minister, he launched "Operation Purgatory" at the end of June 2026. Measured against his fighting talk, little has happened so far. There have been no sweeping purges of the state apparatus, although some government funds flowing to Orban-aligned businessmen have been cut off. Police and prosecutors have summoned a handful of relatively unknown individuals for questioning, and a few people were arrested. The governing majority also established an agency to recover assets, but it is is not yet up and running. But at the beginning of the week, Hungarians witnessed the first significant development in the promised reckoning with the Orban system. Two prominent lawmakers and former ministers were arrested over corruption allegations. On Monday, Magyar's Tisza Party parliamentary faction used its two-thirds majority to lift the immunity of two lawmakers from the opposition Orban camp: Balazs Hanko, formerly minister for culture and innovation and a lawmaker from Orban's Fidesz party, and Miklos Sesztak, a former development minister who is now a lawmaker for the small Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP), which has been a Fidesz affiliate since 2010. Both are the subject of corruption investigations. Former Minister Miklos Sesztak in 2017 Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO Illegal party financing, bribery Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes. The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector. Barricaded in parliament with his family Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule." The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko talks to press after walking out of the National Assembly Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft. In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament. In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?" Dispute over Prosecutor General Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general. The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine . Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings, but could be in the future. How much Orban influence remains in Hungary's politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Hungarians seek a swift reckoning Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state." Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk. Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law. https://www.insidermonkey.com/news/pfize.text: Share On September 13, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that Pfizer Inc. (NYSE: PFE ) is enforcing a Belgian court judgment against Poland and Romania over unpaid COVID-19 vaccine orders by targeting an unusual source of leverage: air traffic control fees. Eurocontrol, the intergovernmental body that coordinates European air traffic management, has frozen transfers of airline route charges owed to Poland’s and Romania’s air navigation agencies. It happened after Pfizer moved to enforce an April court ruling requiring the two countries to pay a combined roughly $2.1 billion for vaccine doses they declined to accept under a 2021 European Union contract. Don’t Miss: Novo Nordisk (NVO) and Eli Lilly (LLY)’s Weight-Loss Drugs Still Work at Smaller Doses, Study Finds Bull Case Pfizer Inc. (NYSE: PFE ) enters the dispute from a strong legal position after winning an enforceable Belgian court ruling. In April, the Brussels court rejected Poland’s and Romania’s arguments for abandoning their pandemic-era purchase commitments. The court ordered them to accept and pay for €1.9 billion, or about $2.2 billion, of Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines. Poland accounts for €1.3 billion of that amount and Romania for €600 million. It gives Pfizer a court-backed claim rather than an unresolved contractual demand. Pfizer’s enforcement effort could protect significant contractual value that Poland and Romania stopped honoring after COVID demand collapsed. Eurocontrol has already withheld air-navigation fees from Poland and imposed a precautionary seizure tied to Romania. It shows that Pfizer has moved beyond simply winning a judgment and has begun using legal mechanisms to pursue collection. Romania’s health minister also said the ruling remains enforceable during an appeal, which strengthens Pfizer’s position even as litigation continues. Pfizer’s overall business reduces the importance of this dispute to its long-term investment case. Second-quarter results beat expectations as Eliquis sales rose 21% to $2.43 billion. Padcev sales climbed 23% to $667 million, helping offset declining COVID-related revenue. Pfizer also raised the lower end of its 2026 revenue outlook and now expects $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion in sales. So any eventual recovery from the vaccine contracts would supplement a business that is already shifting toward non-COVID products. (NYSE: PFE )’s decision to target air-navigation fees creates significant reputational risk even though the company has a court judgment behind it. Poland’s air traffic agency says airline fees provide more than 80% of its income. Polish and Romanian aviation authorities have warned that freezing those funds could threaten essential operations and air safety. Pfizer may have a legal right to pursue payment. However, investors still need to consider the public backlash that can follow aggressive enforcement against infrastructure agencies. Poland and Romania are challenging the rulings, so Pfizer still faces legal uncertainty over the ultimate outcome. Poland has said it will pursue all available legal remedies. Romania has also challenged the enforcement measures. The judgments currently allow Pfizer to seek payment, but successful appeals or changes to the enforcement process could delay collection, return seized funds or prolong the dispute for years. The dispute keeps Pfizer tied to politically sensitive COVID-era contracts just as management works to move the investment story toward newer products and pipeline growth. Pfizer now relies on drugs such as Eliquis, Padcev, and acquired assets to offset declining COVID revenue and upcoming patent expirations. A prolonged public fight with European governments over unwanted vaccine doses could distract from that transition and strain relationships with public-sector customers and policymakers even if Pfizer ultimately prevails in court. Hedge Fund Sentiment Pfizer Inc. (NYSE: PFE )’s hedge fund count held steady at 83 funds in both the second and first quarters, though position value fell to $4.71 billion from $6.15 billion, according to Insider Monkey’s database. Bristol Myers Squibb, a fellow large pharmaceutical company navigating its own portfolio transitions, saw holders decline to 74 from 83, with position value also falling to $4.79 billion from $5.97 billion. Conclusion Pfizer Inc. (NYSE: PFE ) has a strong legal foundation for pursuing Poland and Romania after a Belgian court ordered the two governments to honor roughly $2.2 billion of vaccine commitments. The company has already begun using established enforcement mechanisms to seek payment. Its improving non-COVID portfolio also means the dispute does not define Pfizer’s broader growth strategy. However, targeting air-navigation fees creates reputational and political risk. Ongoing appeals leave uncertainty around the timing and final amount Pfizer may ultimately collect. Investors should look at the dispute as a potentially valuable legal recovery rather than a core earnings driver while watching whether Pfizer can enforce its contracts without damaging important government relationships in Europe.
